interactions.label: Which combination of interventions defines the 'modification' in modified ECT?

params.question: Which combination of interventions defines the 'modification' in modified ECT?

answers.text: General anaesthesia, succinylcholine as a muscle relaxant, and oxygenation with ventilation support

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. These three interventions eliminate the musculoskeletal complications of unmodified ECT — fractures, dislocations — while preserving the therapeutic cerebral seizure.

answers.text: General anaesthesia, anticonvulsant premedication, and continuous cardiac monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Anticonvulsants would suppress the very seizure that makes ECT therapeutic. The three modifications are general anaesthesia, succinylcholine (muscle relaxant), and oxygenation/ventilation.

answers.text: Local anaesthesia to the scalp, oral sedation, and supplemental oxygen via nasal prongs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Modified ECT requires general anaesthesia, not local. The patient must be fully unconscious so that succinylcholine-induced paralysis does not cause distress.

answers.text: Intravenous sedation, bilateral electrode placement, and continuous EEG monitoring

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Electrode placement and EEG monitoring are part of the ECT procedure but are not the three modifications. The modifications specifically address patient safety: general anaesthesia, succinylcholine, and ventilation support.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three modifications that define modern ECT are: (1) short-acting general anaesthesia, (2) succinylcholine as a muscle relaxant, and (3) oxygenation with ventilation support. Together, they prevent the fractures and dislocations seen in unmodified ECT.

Well done. These three modifications — general anaesthesia, succinylcholine, and oxygenation/ventilation — transform ECT from a complication-prone procedure into a safe, controlled treatment with 70–90% response rates in severe depression.

interactions.label: A 28-year-old woman with severe depression has not responded to adequate trials

params.question: A 28-year-old woman with severe depression has not responded to adequate trials of two different antidepressants over eight weeks. Under the ECT indications framework, which category does her case fall into?

answers.text: Urgency — she is at immediate risk of death from the illness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Urgency applies when the patient cannot safely wait for medication to work — e.g., active suicidal intent or refusal to eat. This patient's problem is that medication has been tried and has failed, not that waiting itself is dangerous.

answers.text: Failure — adequate pharmacological treatment has not produced a response

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Two adequate antidepressant trials without response meets the definition of treatment-resistant depression, which falls under the 'failure' arm of the ECT indications framework.

answers.text: Contraindication — antidepressant medications are medically unsafe for her

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 'contraindication' category applies when the medication itself poses a risk — for example, during certain stages of pregnancy. Here the medications were tried safely; they simply did not work.

answers.text: Maintenance — ECT is being used to sustain remission after initial recovery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Maintenance ECT exists but is not part of the three-arm indications framework discussed here. The framework covers urgency (can't wait), failure (medication didn't work), and contraindication (medication is risky).

overallFeedback.feedback: This patient has treatment-resistant depression (two failed adequate trials), classified under the 'failure' category. The three-arm framework is: urgency (can't wait for drugs to work), failure (drugs tried and didn't work), and contraindication (drugs themselves are risky for this patient).

Exactly. Treatment-resistant depression — failure of at least two adequate antidepressant trials — is one of the strongest indications for ECT, classified under the 'failure' arm of the urgency–failure–contraindication framework.

interactions.label: Raised intracranial pressure is an absolute contraindication to ECT.

params.question: Raised intracranial pressure is an absolute contraindication to ECT.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Actually, this statement is false. There are no absolute contraindications to ECT. Raised intracranial pressure, recent myocardial infarction, phaeochromocytoma, and aortic aneurysm all require extra precautions and multidisciplinary involvement, but none absolutely bar ECT when the benefit outweighs the risk.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. There are no absolute contraindications to ECT. Raised intracranial pressure requires extra caution, multidisciplinary involvement, and additional precautions, but it does not rule out ECT when the clinical indication is strong enough to justify the risk.

interactions.label: A colleague asks: 'If succinylcholine prevents the patient from convulsing, how

params.question: A colleague asks: 'If succinylcholine prevents the patient from convulsing, how can ECT still work?' Which explanation is correct?

answers.text: Succinylcholine wears off before the electrical stimulus is applied, so a full motor seizure still occurs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Succinylcholine is specifically timed to be active during the stimulus — abolishing the motor convulsion is the whole purpose of modification, preventing the fractures and dislocations of unmodified ECT.

answers.text: The therapeutic benefit comes from the electrical current itself passing through the brain, independent of any seizure activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The generalised cerebral seizure is the therapeutic mechanism, not the electrical current per se. An adequate seizure lasting at least 25 seconds on EEG must be induced for ECT to be effective.

answers.text: Succinylcholine acts only at the peripheral neuromuscular junction and does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so the cerebral seizure proceeds unimpaired

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Exactly. Succinylcholine paralyses skeletal muscle peripherally but cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. The cerebral seizure — visible on EEG and responsible for the therapeutic effect — occurs normally despite complete motor paralysis.

answers.text: Succinylcholine only partially blocks the motor seizure, preserving enough residual muscle contraction for therapeutic benefit

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: At the dose used in modified ECT, succinylcholine produces near-complete motor paralysis. The therapeutic benefit comes entirely from the cerebral seizure, not from any residual muscle contraction.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: succinylcholine blocks neuromuscular transmission at the peripheral junction only. It cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, so the cerebral seizure — the actual therapeutic mechanism of ECT — proceeds unimpaired and is confirmed on EEG.

Well done. This distinction — motor seizure abolished peripherally, cerebral seizure preserved centrally — is the single most important fact for correcting the misconception that muscle relaxants negate ECT's therapeutic benefit.
